query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by the selective oxidation of Cr and Ti at grain boundaries, which leads to the formation of brittle oxide phases that compromise the fcc matrix integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to oxidizing (e.g., air or oxygen) and reducing (e.g., hydrogen or carbon monoxide) gas environments at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1000°C).
generation.conditions: Controlled gas environments with well-defined oxygen partial pressures and exposure times to isolate oxidation and reduction effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions enriched in Cr and Ti.
generation.mechanism: Cr and Ti preferentially oxidize at grain boundaries due to their higher affinity for oxygen, forming brittle oxides that disrupt the cohesion of the fcc matrix and initiate microcracks.
generation.predicted_outcome: In oxidizing environments, the alloy will exhibit grain boundary oxidation and microcrack formation, leading to reduced mechanical integrity. In reducing environments, the degradation will be less pronounced due to the suppression of oxide formation.
generation.baseline: The starting alloy with an intact fcc matrix and no exposure to elevated-temperature oxidizing or reducing gases.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to temperatures between 800–1000°C and oxygen partial pressures typical of oxidizing and reducing environments. It assumes no significant phase transformation of the fcc matrix during exposure.
generation.uncertainty: The extent of Cr and Ti segregation at grain boundaries and the kinetics of oxide formation under these specific conditions are not fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose samples of the alloy to oxidizing and reducing gas environments at 800–1000°C for varying durations. Use electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to analyze grain boundary regions for oxide formation and microcrack development.
measurements: Grain boundary composition (Cr and Ti content)
Presence and morphology of oxide phases
Mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength, fatigue performance) after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no selective oxidation of Cr and Ti is observed at grain boundaries, or if the mechanical integrity of the alloy is not compromised despite oxide formation, the hypothesis will be falsified.
